t: Wind twisted the Tacoma Narrows Bridge apart
b: In 1940, the Tacoma Narrows Bridge in Washington State twisted wildly in a steady wind and collapsed. It wasn't simple resonance: the wind created self-feeding 'flutter'. Engineers now test bridge designs in wind tunnels.

q.p: What brought down the Tacoma Narrows Bridge?

rq.p: What do engineers do now because of it?

why: Aerodynamic flutter can grow until a structure fails.

b: Mains electricity is alternating current, which flips direction many times a second (50 times in the UK). AC is easy to step up to high voltages for long-distance power lines, which waste less energy, then back down for homes.

q.p: How many times a second does UK mains current change direction?

rq.p: Why is AC used for power grids?
o: Its voltage is easy to change

why: High voltage means less current and less heat lost in wires.

b: Transformers change voltage using two coils of wire around an iron core. A changing current in one coil creates a changing magnetic field, which drives current in the other. More turns in the second coil means a higher voltage.

q.p: What device steps electricity's voltage up or down?

rq.p: Why don't transformers work with steady DC?
o: They need a changing magnetic field

why: Only a changing field induces current in the second coil.

b: A fuse contains a thin wire that melts if too much current flows, breaking the circuit before wires overheat and start a fire. Circuit breakers do the same job but can be reset with a switch.

q.p: What does a fuse do when too much current flows?
o: Its wire melts and breaks the circuit

rq.p: How is a circuit breaker different from a fuse?

why: Too much current heats wires, which can cause fires.

t: UK plugs have a fuse inside
b: British plugs are unusual in containing their own fuse, typically 3 or 13 amps. They also have a longer earth pin that opens shutters in the socket, stopping objects being pushed into the live holes.

q.p: What's unusual inside a UK plug?

rq.p: What does the longer earth pin do?

why: The design dates from post-war wiring standards in 1947.

t: Solar panels make electricity from light
b: Solar cells are made from silicon layers. When light hits them, it knocks electrons loose, and the cell's structure pushes them in one direction, creating a current. Typical home panels convert about 20% of sunlight into electricity.

q.p: What do most solar panels use to make electricity?

rq.p: About how efficient are typical home panels?

why: Light energy frees electrons that then flow as current.

t: Wind turbines turn slowly but strongly
b: Big wind turbine blades look slow, but their tips can move faster than 250 km/h. A gearbox or special generator converts the slow, powerful turning of the rotor into electricity.

q.p: How fast can the tips of large wind turbine blades move?

rq.p: Why do turbines look slow?
o: They're huge, so tips cover great distances
They really are slow at the tips
An optical illusion from the blades' colour

why: The longer the blade, the faster the tip for the same turning rate.

t: Phones know which way is up
b: Phones contain tiny accelerometers, microscopic structures that shift slightly as the phone tilts or moves. Measuring these shifts tells the phone which way gravity is pulling, so the screen can rotate.

q.p: How does your phone know when you rotate it?

rq.p: What force does the accelerometer detect when still?

why: Microscopic parts bend slightly under gravity's pull.

b: Smartphones contain a magnetometer that senses Earth's magnetic field. Map apps combine it with GPS to show which way you're facing. Nearby magnets or metal can confuse it, which is why apps sometimes ask you to wave your phone in a figure of eight.

q.p: Why do map apps ask you to wave your phone in a figure of eight?

rq.p: What sensor works as a phone's compass?

why: Moving it lets the phone separate Earth's field from local interference.

t: Why the 'save' icon is a floppy disk
b: The save icon shows a 3.5-inch floppy disk, a storage format popular in the 1980s and 1990s that held 1.44 MB, less than one phone photo today. The icon stuck long after the disks disappeared.

q.p: What does the classic 'save' icon show?

rq.p: How much could a standard 3.5-inch floppy hold?

why: Familiar symbols outlive the objects they show.

t: Wet phones: rice doesn't help much
b: Putting a wet phone in rice is popular advice, but tests suggest it works no better than leaving the phone to dry in open air. Apple's own guidance advises against rice, partly because small particles can get inside.

q.p: Does putting a wet phone in rice help it dry?
o: Not really, air-drying works as well

rq.p: What does Apple advise against for wet phones?

why: Rice absorbs little moisture from inside a sealed phone.
src: Apple Support: liquid-detection alert on iPhone

b: A plane's 'black box' flight recorders are actually painted bright orange so they're easier to find after a crash. They're built to survive huge impacts and fires, and send an underwater beacon signal.

q.p: What colour is an aeroplane's 'black box'?

rq.p: Why are flight recorders brightly coloured?

why: Visibility matters most when searching wreckage.

b: An early version of the escalator was installed as a novelty ride at Coney Island in 1896. When Harrods installed one in London in 1898, staff reportedly offered nervous customers brandy at the top.

q.p: What did Harrods reportedly offer customers after its first escalator?

rq.p: Where was an early escalator installed as a ride?

why: Moving stairs were thrilling and a little scary at first.

t: Cat's eyes on roads need no power
b: Percy Shaw invented reflective road studs in 1934 in Yorkshire, reportedly inspired by a cat's eyes shining in his headlights. Each stud's rubber casing squeezes down when a car drives over it, wiping the glass clean.

q.p: Who invented 'cat's eyes' road studs?

rq.p: How do cat's eyes stay clean?
o: Rubber wipes them as cars drive over

why: Glass beads reflect headlights straight back to the driver.

b: The first traffic signal was installed outside London's Houses of Parliament in 1868 to control horse-drawn carriages. It was gas-lit and operated by a police officer. It exploded the next year, injuring the officer.

q.p: When was the first traffic signal installed?

rq.p: What happened to the first traffic signal?

why: A gas leak caused the explosion.

b: Studies in shops have found that slower background music can make people walk more slowly and spend more. In one wine shop study, playing French music boosted French wine sales, while German music boosted German wine.

q.p: What did French music do in a wine shop study?

rq.p: What can slow background music encourage?

why: Cues we barely notice can steer choices.

t: Ice is slippery for surprising reasons
b: Many people believe skates melt ice by pressure. The pressure effect is actually far too small. Scientists think a thin, water-like layer naturally exists on ice's surface, and friction from sliding adds more melting.

q.p: Is pressure melting the main reason ice is slippery?
o: No, the effect is too small

rq.p: What do scientists think makes ice slippery?

why: Surface molecules are less tightly bound than those inside.

b: Non-stick coatings are usually PTFE, better known by the brand name Teflon, discovered by accident in 1938 by chemist Roy Plunkett. Its molecules are so slippery that almost nothing can grip them.

q.p: How was Teflon discovered?

rq.p: What is Teflon's chemical name?

why: Fluorine atoms shield its carbon backbone from sticking.

t: Coffee and tea stains form rings
b: When a spilled drop of coffee dries, the edge stays pinned while liquid evaporates fastest there. Fluid flows outward to replace it, carrying coffee particles, which pile up into a dark ring. Physicists call it the coffee ring effect.

q.p: Why do coffee spills dry into rings?
o: Liquid flows to the edge as it evaporates
The cup's rim leaves a mark

rq.p: What do physicists call this?

why: Evaporation is fastest at a drop's thin edge.

b: Firework colours come from metal salts that glow at particular colours when heated: strontium gives red, sodium yellow, barium green and copper blue. Blue is the hardest to make bright.

q.p: What makes the colours in fireworks?

rq.p: Which metal gives fireworks a red colour?

why: Each element gives off its own colours of light when hot.

b: A soap bubble's film pulls inward like a stretched skin. A sphere is the shape that encloses a given amount of air with the least surface area, so surface tension pulls bubbles into spheres.

q.p: Why are bubbles spherical?
o: A sphere has the least surface for its volume

rq.p: What force pulls a bubble into shape?

why: Nature tends to minimise energy, and less surface means less energy.

t: Velcro, zips and buttons: the zip's story
b: Early zip-like fasteners appeared in the 1890s, but Gideon Sundback's improved design in 1913 made them reliable. The name 'zipper' came from a 1920s brand of rubber boots with zip fasteners.

q.p: Where does the name 'zipper' come from?

rq.p: Who made the zip reliable in 1913?

why: Interlocking teeth pulled together by a slider made it work.

t: Why you see stars after standing up fast
b: When you stand up quickly, gravity pulls blood toward your legs and your blood pressure briefly drops. Your brain gets slightly less blood until your body adjusts, which can cause dizziness and spots in your vision.

q.p: Why can standing up fast make you dizzy?

rq.p: What does your body do to fix it?
o: Tightens blood vessels and speeds the heart

why: It takes a few seconds for reflexes to catch up.

b: A hiccup is a sudden contraction of your diaphragm, followed by your vocal cords snapping shut, which makes the 'hic' sound. Common triggers include eating fast, fizzy drinks and excitement. Most bouts stop on their own within minutes.

q.p: What makes the 'hic' sound?

rq.p: Which muscle spasms in a hiccup?

why: The closing vocal cords cut off the sudden breath in.

b: Seeing, hearing or even reading about yawning can make you yawn. Studies find people are more likely to catch yawns from family and friends than from strangers, though why we yawn at all is still debated.

q.p: Who are you most likely to 'catch' a yawn from?

rq.p: Do scientists fully understand why we yawn?
o: Yes, it cools the brain only

why: Contagious yawning may be linked to social bonding.
